utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic, also known as "Vlado."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The Prosecution is represented today by Mr. Albert Moskowitz, Mr. Blaxil and myself. I should like to add for the information of the Tribunal that Mr. Moskowitz is leaving us at the end of this week to resume important duties in his own country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Ranko Radovic appearing on behalf of Zoran Kupreskic, and my co-counsel is Mr. Tomislav Pasaric, so allow me to introduce him to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. My name is attorney Slokovic-Glumac. I'm representing Mr. Mirjan Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Borislav Krajina, and I'm representing the accused Vlatko Kupreskic. My co-counsel is my colleague Zelimir Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Luko Susak representing Drago Josipovic, and allow me to introduce Goranka Herljevic my co-counsel. She's an attorney from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Petar Pavkovic, Defence counsel for Vladimir Santic, and allow me to introduce my legal assistant Mr. Mirko Vrdoljak, attorney from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm attorney Petar Puliselic appearing on behalf of Dragan Papic. My co-counsel is Ms. Nika Pinter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So I see there is a good news and bad news. Good news is that Counsel Radovic is back with us, and we are very pleased to see that he is in good shape, and I hope that he has fully recovered. The bad news is that Mr. Moskowitz is leaving. I'm sure that we all, both the Court and Defence counsel, and also your colleagues in the Prosecution's office will miss your competence, and your wit and wisdom, and also your sense of balance. I'm very sorry that you're leaving. I also would like to welcome the co-counsel who have been appointed over the holiday, and Mr. Blaxill, who I understand is appearing for the Prosecution. Now, before we start with our proceedings, let me say a few things and we'll touch upon some housekeeping matters. First of all, we have agreed that the court calendar for the period January-March will be as follows, from 9.00 to 1.30 in the morning, every morning, and I propose that we take a break -- first break at 10.30. So we'll be sitting from 9.00, from 9.00 sharp, to 10.30, then a break from 10.30 to 10.50. We resume at 10.50 and go on to 12.10. Then we have a break, a second break, and then we start again at 12.30 until 1.30. However, we must make some exceptions. There may be some problems on -- we can't sit on Thursday because of some personal problems. So, therefore, I suggest we sit on Wednesday both in the morning and in the afternoon. I'm sorry about that, because I understand that this is going to be a bit difficult, particularly for Defence counsel, but this is a way of not wasting time. We will let you know when we'll be sitting on Wednesday, the precise hours in the morning and in the afternoon. Also, next Monday, as you may know, it's a new UN Holiday, so we will not be sitting next Monday. So this week we'll be sitting Monday and Tuesday, according to the normal schedule of our Trial Chamber, then Wednesday both morning and the afternoon, no sitting on Thursday, and morning sitting on Friday. Then we will resume Tuesday of next week. Let me move on to a few other matters. First of all, a request for the granting of safe conduct for Josip Kolic was made by Defence counsel, and I wonder whether the Prosecutor has any comment on this request. Before we issue an order of this matter we would like to check with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We have no comment, Mr. President. We leave it up to the judgement of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Therefore, we will issue the safe conduct for Josip Kolic. This will be done today. Second and most serious problem, I see that there are more than 140 witnesses who are going to be called by the Defence, and there are very many, and so we are wondering whether we could find a way of reducing the number of witnesses. I mean, of course, if Defence counsel are prepared to do so. Let me, first of all, read the -- read out the text of a new Rule of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence that was adopted recently and which might prove of some help. I don't know whether you have received the document issued by the Registry on the 10th of December containing a set of new Rules of Procedure which have come into force on the 17th of December. Now, this Rule I'm thinking of is Rule 94 ter called Affidavit Evidence. Affidavit Evidence. I will read it slowly: "To prove a fact in dispute, a party may propose to call a witness and to submit in corroboration of his or her testimony on that fact affidavits signed by other witnesses in accordance with the law and procedure of the State in which such affidavits are signed. These affidavits are admissible if the other party does not object within five working days after the witness' testimony. If the party objects and the Trial Chamber so rules, or if the Trial Chamber so orders, the witnesses shall be called for cross-examination." I think this is an important Rule which might prove useful for the purpose of expediting proceedings in our Tribunal. In particular, I'm thinking -- I'm wondering -- we Judges are wondering whether this Rule could be applied to the various character witnesses Defence counsel intends to call. I wonder whether Defence counsel could consider the possibility of just producing one character witness and then affidavits emanating from other character witnesses so that we don't need to call them. Of course, as long as the Prosecution does not object. This is an area where the new Rule 94 ter could be applied, and probably also other areas. In addition, there are some queries I would like to now set out. There are some -- after reading carefully all the witness statements produced by the Defence, we have come across some statements emanating from witnesses who may not be necessary. I mean, let me just point to them. Sorry, there are so many documents that it's very difficult to find the relevant ones. Yes. These are some witnesses Defence counsel for Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic intend to call. I will mention their names. All of them, according to their written statements, report about the TV report concerning Sakib Ahmic and the interview he gave on TV. They simply say, "I was there. I watched that TV report and this is what he said." Now, since we have been given by the Prosecution the TV cassette, is it necessary to call those four witnesses? I'm referring to Ilija Zrezic, Anto Rajic, Niko Sakic (phoen), and Mirko Safradin. It's just a suggestion for the consideration of Defence counsel for Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic. Another point relates to the question of persecution, Count 1. Again, after reading carefully the various witness statements, as well as the trial brief produced on this matter, on legal issues, by Defence counsel for Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic, we are wondering to what extent some statements are relevant to the issues in dispute in this particular case. Let me explain what I mean by that. Some Defence witnesses's statements allege that Croats were persecuted by Muslims, in some particular areas, in some villages. Now, we're wondering what the relevance of this evidence would be. If it is a tu quoque evidence, tu quoque evidence, namely evidence that is intended to show that also the other side committed similar crimes, then this is not material, because as you know, this Defence is not relevant. It's not a Defence in International Law. Now, I think to see from some Defence Counsel that it is not tu 1 quoque evidence, but then the Court would ask the Defence to explain the relevance of this type of evidence touching upon the issue of persecution, so that we are clear about the aim of the Prosecution. Now, let me just, before I give the floor to Counsel Radovic on this matter, wind up my sort of introductory set of comments by raising a final issue. I think we agreed that we should proceed as follows: Count by count. So we would start with Count 1, and then after we have completed the hearings on Count 1 we will move on to the other counts. Now, if this is so, are Defence counsel prepared to make opening statements only on Count 1, so each count as we go along, because I think this will be the most -- from the viewpoint of judicial economy, the most helpful approach, also the most orderly one, first of all to dispose of the count and then move on to the next count, and then at that stage hearing opening statements of Defence counsel on that particular count, or do Defence counsel intend to make opening statements on all counts this week? So this, again, is a question. Therefore, I will now stop and ask Counsel Radovic to address these two issues, the question of persecution and how Defence counsel intend to proceed on the various counts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I respond in the same order in which the President has spoken? That is, I would begin with the witnesses referring to that TV programme. We were grateful to the Prosecutor having obtained this video cassette having to do with the statement of Sakib Ahmic that he made for Zenica television in the hospital in Zenica. However, it is our assertion that this tape did not contain the whole programme. After that, the Prosecution obtained a lengthier tape, that is one that had a longer introduction than on the previous tape. However, we are still claim this is not the complete tape, and these witnesses need to confirm that Sakib Ahmic made a lengthier statement and that the journalist who interviewed him told -- that he told this journalist that he didn't know which persons had broken into his home, because those persons wore masks. So we agree that there is no dispute that he gave an interview, there is no dispute the TV programme in which he appeared, but what is disputed is whether this tape is complete, and that is why we continue to need these witnesses. Maybe not all four of them, but at least two, and these two should at least tell us everything that they saw on that programme. As regards the witnesses having to do with other areas and not necessarily the area of Ahmici itself, we decided to call these witnesses for two reasons. The first is that the Prosecutor also called and questioned witnesses who spoke about events outside Ahmici and outside the region of Busovaca. My colleague Madam Slokovic-Glumac and myself objected at the time to this line of questioning, as it had no relevance to the position of our clients, but the Tribunal rejected our objection because they explained that they needed to be acquainted with the developments within the Lasva Valley as a whole, and, therefore, if the Prosecution brought witnesses to speak about what happened in a broader region, then we have to do the same so as to give the Trial Chamber a full impression of what was happening, because the conflict did not occur only in Ahmici, nor did it begin in Ahmici but in another area and sometime prior to Ahmici. Furthermore, an important section of our Defence regarding the second count and partly the first count as well has to do with intent. We know, from the Tadic case, that the concept of intent is rather broadly interpreted in this Tribunal, but our Defence is that our clients were not aware of the conflict that was being prepared, and when they were informed after midnight on the 16th of April that they had to evacuate civilians because an attack was being prepared by the Muslim forces, and because of the events occurring in the surroundings of Vitez and a little further away where the Muslims were attacking Croats, this fact, in the consciousness of the accused, necessarily gave them the impression that the information they received was correct, and we will bring a witness to tell us how they received these instructions to evacuate the civilians. That is the reason were we are talking about events that occurred beyond Ahmici itself, because news of those events reached Ahmici. Ahmici was not an island in the middle of nowhere, it was part of an area which was the scene of conflict. As for the opening statements of the Defence, I must admit that I, together with my colleague, Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac, had intended to give a complete opening statement because one thing leads to another, because if we talk about the interpersonal relations and the events occurring beyond Vitez and in the surroundings of Vitez, then this immediately leads to the events of the 15th and the 16th, rather early in the morning of the 16th, and the intent of our clients and the movements of our clients. In addition to this, we have another request beyond the opening remarks you have made. In our State, we have to report our incomes by the end of February, which means that we have to fill in our tax returns, and if the trial is not completed by the 21st of February, could you please make a break between the 21st and the 28th of February to give us time to fill in our tax forms which we have to do under the law? That is all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Regarding the extent to which we will go into the persecution count, I should like to say that in the background it says that on the 16th of April, a coordinated attack was carried out on all villages in an area of ten kilometres around Vitez, and certain locations are listed there in the indictment, Sivrino Selo, Preocica, Santici, Nadioci, Ahmici, but also other villages like Bila, Kruscica, Gacice, and in those villages, the Prosecutor has not proven the existence of a conflict, and a part of our defence is to show what was actually happening in those villages on that day; and I think that in the course of the Prosecution case, you did ask what was happening in the other villages. The distance between these villages is only a couple of kilometres, and they are all within a range of ten kilometres from Vitez, and therefore, I think, to have an overall idea of what was happening, how the BH army was organised, how it acted, how the HVO acted in this whole area, and in order to be able to assess the situation there and what happened in Ahmici, we have to call these witnesses. It is a fact that these witnesses only mention in passing what actually happened to them on that day. One event that is rather unique is the crime in Dusina but it is a part of the Busovaca war which occurred on the 24th of January, '94, and we wish to use this case to show how the BH army was organised, how it was structured, and to give an overview of what happened later on in Vitez. We will not exaggerate, however, with these witnesses. There won't be too many testimonies about those events. We have only two witnesses about it. But as to the events in Vitez itself on the 16th, I consider that to be part of our defence which cannot be bypassed because we wish to show how and why the events in Ahmici actually occurred. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any comments from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The Prosecution would like to make some comments upon the resumption of this trial and to convey some concerns it has after the information communicated to us by the Defence attorneys.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: No translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: There is no B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I will repeat, Mr. President. I was saying that the Prosecution would like to convey to the Tribunal and the representatives of the Defence some of its concerns. First of all, regarding the information communicated to us prior to the resumption of these hearings by the Defence attorneys. We received a certain amount of information about the witnesses that will be called by the Defence; very few statements signed by witnesses but many summaries. We regret in particular that many of the summaries that we received are in an extreme summary form and give no real indication of the purpose of the testimony which will be solicited from those witnesses. It appears to us, therefore, that the principle of equality of arms between the parties here present in the Tribunal is being called in question, and it seems to us that for the trial to continue to evolve under good conditions, it is absolutely desirable that a correction be made by the Tribunal regarding this situation. What we suggest, therefore, in this connection is that the Tribunal authorises the Prosecution to hear the witnesses that will be called by the Defence before their appearance here in court. I wish to specify that this is in order to correct the situation in which we find ourselves today and to guarantee the principle of equality of arms between parties. I would add that the Prosecution, of course, does not intend to interview all the witnesses that the Defence intends to call but only some of them, specifically those who may speak in direct contradiction with the testimony that the Tribunal has already heard and, of course, we do not wish to force a witness to speak to the Prosecution; of course, it will depend upon the agreement of the witnesses. We cannot force any of them. We would like the Witness Protection Unit to be the intermediary between the Prosecution and the witnesses and that this unit see whether each witness is willing or not to be interviewed by the Prosecution before appearing in court. A second point of concern of the Prosecution has to do with the defence of Mr. Vlado Santic. Due to the extremely summarised form of the communication conveyed to us, it seems to us that many of the witnesses that the Defence of Vlado Santic intends to call before the Tribunal are going to speak to the defence of alibi because five or six witnesses apparently were in Vitez on the 16th of April and will tell us what they saw without any further precision. Under those conditions, and in view of the information that has been communicated to us, we fear that these witnesses will come to the Tribunal to say that the accused was not in Ahmici but in Vitez on the 16th of April in the morning, and we wish to remind the Defence counsel of Mr. Santic of the Rules regarding the defence of alibi, and especially the ruling on the 17th of August when this question was referred to in detail and precision. If Vlado Santic wishes to establish before the Tribunal that he was not in Ahmici in the morning of the 16th of April, he can do so, of course, but not through witnesses and only by his own deposition before the Tribunal. This brings me to the third point of concern which I wish to convey to the Tribunal. We have not been informed by the Defence counsel whether the accused intend or do not intend to testify themselves in the course of these proceedings. Of course, the decision is fully up to them, but it seems to me that it would have been fair, upon the resumption of this trial, that we be informed of the decision of each of the accused so that we might know whether any one of those clients will testify in court. This would give us a chance to prepare for the cross-examination of some of the witnesses in a different way, and maybe the Tribunal would consider it appropriate to address this question to Defence counsel today. A fourth and last point of concern that we have has to do with the Rule of customary usage which was prescribed by your Tribunal for the Prosecution and the Prosecution witnesses and which I think needs to be reiterated when it comes to the Defence witnesses; specifically, the Rule that at the end of a week, we should have a list of witnesses for the following week, and I must say that on Friday, I thank Madam Glumac for the list of witnesses that we received for this week, and if new witnesses are being called by the Defence, we would like to have a certain time between being notified of the name of that witness and his actual appearance in court so that we can prepare. A delay of 30 days was envisaged for the Prosecution in favour of the Defence. We are not insisting on thirty days, but we would like to have ten or fifteen days to be able to prepare for the cross-examination. I would also like to say that last Friday, a witness that will be called this week, we were told of this witness, but we, to this day, have no indications regarding this witness, we have no information about this witness, and last Friday, we received only very limited information about this witness, it is Vlado Divkovic, who was not mentioned, announced by any of the Defence counsel, and therefore, it seems to us very difficult for this witness to be called to testify this week in view of the very limited time that the Prosecution has to prepare for the cross-examination. My final wish that I should like to convey to the Tribunal, if the Defence will give up some witnesses, that it should let us know as soon as possible so that we can avoid any unnecessary research and waste of time. Those are the points that the Prosecution wish to make to the Trial Chamber upon the resumption of these hearings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I will try to take up the various points made first by Defence counsel and then by the Prosecutor. Now, I do understand what Counsel Radovic said about the tape, and the four witnesses, we would be appreciative if the four witnesses could be reduced to two, but I see you have a point there, a good point, on the particular question of the tape, because I understand the tape you were provided is not complete. All right. This is granted. As for the question of persecution and the need to go beyond what happened in Ahmici, we consider that developments outside of Ahmici before and possibly even after the 16th of April, '93, are relevant to two particular issues: (1) The question of whether or not there was an armed conflict; and (2), whether the alleged crimes can be regarded as crimes against humanity, the crimes allegedly committed in Ahmici could be regarded as crimes against humanity. As we all know, for a crime against humanity to materialise, you need various legal ingredients, and in particular, a widespread or systematic practice, so a particular fact must be part and parcel of a practice. Therefore, the Prosecution I think was right in touching upon events occurring prior to April '93 and outside Ahmici because it is the claim of the Prosecution that some of those facts are to be regarded as crimes against humanity, so as a part of a practice. Any particular persecution, according to the Prosecution, is a crime against humanity; therefore, this general practice, according to the Prosecution, did exist. But these are the only two issues to which anything outside Ahmici, the particular events in Ahmici, may be material. Now, if you say that since the Prosecution was allowed to acquaint the Court with developments in the Lasva Valley as a whole, and therefore, as a result, the Defence is entitled to do likewise, in a way you go beyond, I think, the province of our particular case, the scope of our case, which is again to stick to the points made by the Prosecution and to see whether the Prosecutor is right in claiming that these were crimes against humanity. In particular, those statements which deal with persecution, alleged persecution, of Croats by Muslims as such are not relevant to our case - they may be relevant to other cases, future cases or present cases brought before our Tribunal - where, as I say, Muslims, individual accused, are charged with persecution of Croats. These are different cases. But in our case, as I say, we should try to focus on what I have just said. This is our position. You, of course, are at liberty to produce evidence on other events outside Ahmici, but I do hope that you will confine yourselves to these particular legal issues because otherwise, that evidence would be outside the scope of our case. As for the opening statement, we understand that at least you, Counsel Radovic and Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, intend to make full opening statements dealing with all the various cases, and we're prepared to hear your opening statements -- so once and for all, we will cover the whole range of issues which arise with regards to your clients. We are, however, wondering whether also the other Defence counsel intend to make similar opening statements this week, or whether they prefer to put off their opening statements when we -- until we take up the other counts. It is for you to decide. I mean, we are open to any suggestion. We don't want to impose any particular solution. Let us try, together, to find the particular solution which is more practical and more helpful from the viewpoint of, as I say, judicial economy and for the purpose of conducting expeditious proceedings. Let me stop here because I see you have quickly consulted. Let me ask you how you intend to proceed with the opening statements before I move on to the comments made by the Prosecution? Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this issue of the opening statements, as well as any other questions raised by the Prosecution merit more attention, and I would like to request to allow us, after the first break, to consult during the break and then I'll come back with our comments on these issues in order not to interrupt the hearing now. We will, obviously, take into consideration your request for an expeditious proceeding, and we will try to adapt our opening statements to that, and maybe it is -- it may be best to proceed in the way you have just suggested. In other words, to focus on Count 1 and then on, but I would still request that we be given more time to consult. We will come back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. However, we have already made up our mind on the various four points of concern raised by the Prosecution. Do you want to comment on these four points of concern before we make a ruling on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President. The Prosecution, in these four points, did address a number of points which are common to all defences, but some of them touch only on the accused Vladimir Santic's Defence. I don't know whether this is the right moment to address those specific issues. If you feel that it is, I can proceed, but I can also wait until after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it's only fair for all of you to consult on those four points because some of them are major points and I think you may decide to take a common stand. So let us put off any ruling on this matter until after the coffee break. We will then, first of all, hear your comments, objections or remarks, and then we will, in light of your reaction, make a ruling on those four points. So we can now -- if there are no other matters, we may now start with the opening statement of Counsel Radovic. Yes, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would just like to explain our situation for a moment regarding the evidence which you deem not relevant. You have not yet heard the concept of our defence, and the -- we only provided very summary statements. The Prosecution was referring to a particular practice which he believed was discriminatory regarding the widespread nature of the crimes which then went to qualify as crimes against humanity. However, with respect to all the events which the Prosecutor mentioned as part of this discriminatory procedure, we want to use these witnesses to prove that such practices not exist, at least not in the way it was presented by the Prosecution. So we cannot only address Ahmici but every event which was brought up by the Prosecution during the presentation of their evidence, and we want to offer a different interpretation of these events, and we would like to use the witnesses for that in order to find the truth, in order to find out whether this practice existed, whether it was as widespread as it has been alleged, and whether it rises to the level of crimes against humanity. We believe that we need to be allowed to present that evidence. If we talk about the event which was outside of Vitez, in Dusina, it was ten kilometres. It is another municipality, that is true. However, it is the same region. So we believe that the Defence would be put at a disadvantage. So what my colleague Radovic said about the intent, I think that we need to take these additional aspects in order to arrive at the full picture of what actually transpired. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I see that we are coming to the same point, and I fully agree with you, namely that since the Prosecution claims that this persecution was a widespread practice occurring not only in Ahmici but also outside Ahmici, you are entitled, of course, to prove the contrary, namely that there was no persecution of Muslims by Croats in villages other than Ahmici. I agree with you. But our point was that this -- what is not relevant, we consider, is to prove that there was also persecution by Muslims of Croats. This is not to the point. You have to prove that there was no persecution by Croats of Muslims outside Ahmici. If you can prove this point, then, of course, you may prove that there was no crime against humanity, because this is one of the legal ingredients, the practice, the widespread or systematic practice is lacking. So, therefore, we come to the same point, I think we're concluding. Again, let me now ask both of you whether you are prepared to start with the opening statement. We have 30 minutes and then we could have a break. Probably each of you needs more than 30 minutes, but it would be a waste of time to take a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, given that you have given us certain points which we need to consult on in order to provide answers, maybe it would be better to maybe break now so that we consult and our co-ordinator would then be able to respond to all the issues raised. Following that I can give the opening statement, and I can actually provide an opening statement, and to use a phrase, we can kill two birds with one stone, so that maybe we can wrap it altogether faster. As far as the Prosecutor's request is concerned, whether the investigators will be given -- will give the statement as witnesses, I can give you -- actually, the accused -- the Kupreskic brothers have written to the Tribunal, and they have offered to surrender, and now they are in the phase of the trial where they can present their evidence and they can also provide their own comments on it. We know that no two witnesses will talk about the same event the same way. As far as Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic are concerned, in the nature of their co-operation with the Tribunal, they are prepared to testify on their own behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you made a good suggestion. Let us now break for 20 minutes, and we will resume at twenty-five past ten sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence has considered all the issues and we have a unified position which is as follows: Regarding the first point and the objection by the Prosecution that they received summary statements of the Defence witnesses, the Defence would like to point out the following -- and connected to this issue is the request of the Prosecution to be allowed by the Trial Chamber to talk to the Defence witnesses in order to compensate for the lack of information which is not contained in the summaries. The Defence is -- vigorously objects to any contact of the Defence witnesses with the Prosecution. There are at least three reasons which justify this position of the Defence. Number one, the Prosecution invoked the equality of arms in the proceeding, and says that they provided comprehensive information and evidence through witnesses which they produced. This is not so. We are witness to the fact that some Prosecution witnesses talked about events which the Defence heard for the first time in the open court. Should the Prosecution's request be granted and be allowed to -- contact with the Defence witnesses, this so-called equality of arms would not exist. Secondly, pursuant to the Statute Article 21(3) and the Convention 3 of the Geneva Conventions regarding the presumed innocence, the accused, that is the Defence, is not obliged to do anything in order to help the Prosecution to prove the guilt of an accused. In other words, the request of the Prosecution, should it be granted, would violate these fundamental principles of the criminal proceedings. Thirdly, the third reason, at a Status Conference of 16 October of last year, it was concluded that the Defence did not have an obligation to provide full witness statements but only summaries thereof, and this is what the Defence did and we feel we have complied with the ruling of the Court. So this is in response to the first point. As a long-time Prosecutor, I understand the concern of the Prosecution. If I were in their place, I would be concerned too, but the concern is one thing the right is another thing. The rights of the accused should not and must not be violated. Regarding the second issue, let me skip it for now. This was the issue raised by the Prosecution, which was directed to the Defence of Vlado Santic. I would like to come back to that in closing, but let me move on to the issue of the opening statements. The Defence counsel are in agreement that they should provide the opening statement as part of the whole, because this is how they were preparing for their Defence. We believe that this would facilitate the proceedings and that they would contribute to the general point -- requirement of expediency. As far as the witness list is concerned, we believe that the Defence will be able to provide it to the Prosecution by the last day of the week, a witness list which it intends to call next week. So, Your Honours, my apologies. As far as the issue raised by the Prosecution whether the accused would testify, in addition to what Mr. Radovic said, the other Defence counsel, at this point, have not decided firmly whether their clients would also testify or not. Mr. President, Your Honours, this is the position of the Defence regarding these common issues. I don't know whether you want me to now present the position of the Defence of Mr. Santic with respect to the question raised by the Prosecutor. If I understood him correctly, as part of the objection to the summary statements of Defence witnesses for Mr. Santic, I would like to point out that one could conclude from these summary statements that Mr. Santic is going to invoke an alibi defence, and I would like to make a further comment. The only person, the Prosecution witness, who places Mr. Santic, on 16th of April, in Ahmici is the only witness to do so. When I make my opening statements I will address this in more detail, but the Defence would like to point out, and it also has done so by providing evidence in the earlier part of the trial. This witness's credibility is in question. In other words, the Defence will point out that Mr. Santic was not in Ahmici on 16 April, 1993, but with respect to his whereabouts on that day, the Defence does not have an obligation to provide that evidence. When addressing the intent of the Defence, we said that if necessary, we will point out the location of Mr. Santic on that day. So in short, Your Honours, these are our comments with respect to the issues raised by the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. May I ask you to clarify one particular point, the one about the opening statements? If I understood you correctly, all Defence counsel intend to make opening statements this week. I'm not clear also, after reading the transcript, about what you suggested. Opening statements by all Defence counsel this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: From now until the end -- today. We start today. I don't know whether we will finish today. We could go on if we're not done by the end of the day, we'll continue tomorrow, and we will address all the issues -- all the counts starting with number 1, and depending on what the different counts for each counsel are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will now rule on the various issues raised by the Prosecution, but later on we will issue an order where we give reasons for this ruling and set out those reasons more clearly. First of all, on the crucial issue of witness statements produced by Defence counsel. We also, members of this Trial Chamber, were struck by the excessively summary fashion and succinct way of presenting those statements. They don't enable even the Court to have an idea of what the witness is going to say. In view of the principle of equality of arms, which means that both parties, the Defence and the Prosecution, must be on the same footing, we feel that those statements, some of those statements, are not satisfactory. We also feel that what Defence Counsel Pavkovic said about the principle whereby the Defence should not do anything to help the Prosecution, I think this is a misunderstanding of the principle of equality of arms and the whole spirit of our proceedings. The Prosecution needs detailed statements because the Prosecution must be in a position to cross-examine witnesses. For the same reason, the Prosecution was duty-bound to produce detailed statements of witnesses, so that Defence counsel were in a position to cross-examine. It is not a question of helping the Prosecution, it is a question of helping the Court reaching the truth and deciding on this matter. In view of that, we will ask the Prosecution to produce, maybe by tomorrow, if possible, a list of those witnesses for whom they feel that no satisfactory statements were produced by the Defence. Then the Defence will have two weeks to provide the Prosecution and the Court with detailed statements. If those statements are not provided within two weeks, then the Prosecution will be allowed to interview the various witnesses at issue. But, of course, we would prefer that the Defence provide those detailed statements. As the Prosecutor said, this does not apply to all witnesses; to some of them. But for those witnesses, and we will, I hope, tomorrow get a list of those witnesses, we very much hope that Defence will produce detailed statements within two weeks. Now, the Court is also wondering whether Defence counsel could decide as soon as possible whether or not accused other than Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic are going to testify. We would welcome a response maybe by next Tuesday, as soon as possible, because we also are keen to know the list of witnesses. We grant the motion of the Prosecution to the effect that by each Friday, Defence counsel should provide a list of the witnesses to be called the following week, and I think it is quite appropriate that the Prosecution should be notified ten days in advance of the names of the witnesses to be called so that they can prepare for cross-examination. The Prosecution also asked that the Defence should notify both the Prosecution and the Defence of the names of those witnesses they are going to give up, they are not going to call, and I think we also would appreciate having this list as soon as possible. Coming to the question of Vlado Santic, I think, if I understood the translation correctly, Counsel Pavkovic admitted that this is a defence of alibi, an alibi defence, and under our Rule 67, the defence of alibi is governed by sub-Rule (A)(ii), which applies to a period prior to the commencement of the trial. Now, if this is an alibi defence, and I understand that this is an alibi defence, this Rule has not been complied with by the Defence counsel in this particular case, and then we would apply (B), sub-Rule 67(B), which reads as follows: "Failure of the defence to provide notice under this Rule shall not limit the right of the accused to testify on the above defences," which means that the accused is not duty-bound to testify but has a right to testify, and I think it would be quite appropriate for him to testify on this particular matter. As I say, we will issue an order on all these questions so as to clarify the situation. We will now move on to the various opening statements. We accept the suggestion of Defence counsel that all Defence counsel should make opening statements today and tomorrow, so we will start, I think, with Counsel Radovic, but first of all, let me give the floor to Counsel Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. A part of the Prosecution's comments were not addressed, but I would like to bring it up. We have some problems which the Prosecution also had, that certain witnesses give up at the last moment, like Vlado Divkovic. For instance, his statement -- in fact, we did not take a statement from him, but we indicated what he was going to testify to. He is going to testify on a very narrow issue which has to do with certain documents which have to do with the SPS and the Vitezit companies in Vitez, the big companies in this town, and he is going to show the employee lists in order to prove that there was no discrimination. These documents could be very useful for both the Defence and the Prosecution. So in his case, I would like to ask for an exception. He was -- Mr. Krusanovic, who was going to testify to that, has declined to come, and Mr. Divkovic is going to be absent for a long time and he can only come in a particular time period. So I would like to urge you to try to rule so that this witness can show in a time period when he can, and it is a very limited testimony regarding these documents that have to do with the employee list. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are speaking of Vlado Divkovic who was due to testify this week.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So you are insisting that he should be allowed to testify this week. I wonder whether the Prosecutor has any objection in view of the limited scope of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I have no objection regarding this testimony, the more so as this -- however, this name was communicated to us for the first time last Friday, and we only have a very brief summary of six lines about his statement, and I think that his name will be placed on the list that we will submit to you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise, but we cannot provide any lengthier statement because we haven't even talked to Vlado Divkovic. But we know, because of the position he held, that he would be able to confirm the names of the people employed and the executive posts held in these three enterprises which were later merged to form one, so he will be not testifying about any other circumstances except about the composition of the staff, of the personnel, of these factories, and as the Prosecution will be given the documents, the witness will just confirm the authenticity of those documents and that is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask you whether these documents could be passed on to the Prosecution today or tomorrow so that they can, in a way, waive their right to have a detailed statement? This, in a way, could replace the statement, also because you have already indicated the subject of his testimony. So if you, Mr. Terrier, know now what he is going to talk about and also are provided a document, probably you could refrain from objecting to this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am not objecting to this witness. I wish to be informed as much as possible, in view of the principle of equality of arms, about the contents of the testimony. As was told us today by Madam Glumac, this testimony does not seem to be at all material to our proceedings. We have not conveyed to the Tribunal any information about the names of the people employed in SPS and Vitezit, and I don't see how this testimony is in any sense relevant to the counts and the charges against the accused. If the witness is only going to testify about the staff of these companies where he worked, I really don't need any additional information. I am just asking whether this testimony will be at all useful, and I am not objecting if the Trial Chamber insists on hearing this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: If I understood Madam Glumac, this will be a witness who will be testifying about non-discrimination in these enterprises; therefore, this question is relevant because it has to do with the problem of persecution. Therefore, they are saying that there was no persecution because there was no discrimination in those enterprises; and therefore, I think it is admissible, so I would thank you if you would waive your insistence on having a written text of his statement. You will just be given lists of the employees. You already know what the witness is going to speak to, and so there is no doubt that you will be able to cross-examine that witness and hear him this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The Prosecution will be guided by the decision of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: May I just say that I will be able to provide the Prosecution with the documents already this afternoon, and we have announced those documents in our list of documents submitted to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. So shall we now start with opening statements, and I assume they will be fairly short opening statements, but you are, of course, entitled to touch upon all those issues of law and fact which you consider important or relevant. Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In my opening statement, I shall focus mainly on matters of fact whereas I think we should leave matters of law for the closing statement, at least that is the conception of my opening statement which I am making on behalf of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic since their lives as brothers and the fact that they lived in the same locality, only in different houses, were more or less the same. When we received the amended indictment from the Prosecution of the International Criminal Tribunal for war crimes committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, we were confronted with major difficulties because the indictment in content differed significantly from the kind of indictments we are accustomed to in our legal system, and also in the legal system customary in the Germanic States of Europe, and I think the situation is similar in Italy. I'm not familiar with the situation in France. Namely, what we would describe as factual descriptions, the Prosecution does not give any factual descriptions. By way of example, in the part of the indictment regarding persecution, the Prosecution says that this applies to the period from October 1992 until April 1993 without indicating a single fact that may have occurred between the 1st of October and the end of April 1993 which would be necessary in order to charge the accused for events committed in that period. Then the Prosecutor goes on to allege that the accused persecuted the Bosnian Muslims, the inhabitants of Ahmici and Santici and the environs; therefore, it is not focused exclusively on Ahmici and Santici but also the environs, the persecution being done on political, racial, and religious grounds, without indicating, for any one of the accused, in which way the accused persecuted the Muslims in Ahmici and Santici, and particularly not how they persecuted them in the environs of Ahmici and Santici. When one talks about the environs, one may refer to Vitez and all the other localities that we intend to cover in the course of our case and which the Prosecution mentions in the background of the indictment -- or, rather, in the general allegations. Then the Prosecution goes on to claim that the persecution was done on political, religious, and racial grounds without saying how they did it. Persons who had no political powers or positions, who had no military powers or military positions, how these people could have planned, organised, and executed attacks in order to cleanse all Bosnian Muslims from a village, a particular village and the surrounding areas, for somebody to be able to implement and plan and organise something, he has to have a particular position in the hierarchy of power, and these accused were at the bottom of the pyramid of power; and therefore, any planning, either political or military, was beyond their possibilities. It is particularly unclear what they could have done in the surrounding areas, and concerning those surrounding areas, we have already heard the Prosecution witnesses. To this is added the deliberate and systematic killing of Bosnian Muslims, the destruction of homes and property, and the organised detention and expulsion of Bosnian Muslims. In our system, if such an indictment were to be compiled, the main objection would be that instead of factual descriptions, legal descriptions are given, which means that provisions are being cited from the Statute as incriminations. In simple terms, this would be a bone without the meat because we need to have the meat to understand the whole issue. Because of such a structure of the indictment, the Defence plans in its case to prove, like the Prosecution, the general circumstances of the events in the Lasva Valley, and we are forced to do so because of such an approach taken by the indictment, and we will try to do this with the help of witnesses and documents in the same way that the Prosecution has done. We shall prove the development of the Muslim Territorial Defence and how it grew and developed into the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as the creation and development of the HVO and all this in the area of the Lasva River Valley. We shall also present evidence to show that from the very beginning of the formation of these armed units, the BH army and the HVO did not act together and were not even organisationally united at higher levels of control and command; and even when they engaged in operations against the Serbs, which was, for a time, one of their common objectives in Vlasic, Gornji Vakuf and Komar, the commands were not made jointly, the units were not structured jointly, but rather the units acted separately side by side, so that often there was confusion as to which should do what. We shall also present evidence to show that in the Lasva Valley, there were two armies being formed based on the territorial principle. This is something that we have already heard about during the Prosecution case. Something else that we consider important for developments in this area was that in the month of September 1992, the civilian authorities broke down which were based on the results of the free elections. The Muslims separated and created their own authorities. First, The Coordination Committee for the Protection of Muslims and then the War Presidency with all the attributes of power. Therefore, in that territory, there were two armies, two military police forces, two civilian police forces, two Defence secretariats or Defence departments, and two separate structures of civilian authority. In such a situation, the circumstances were further complicated with the advent of a large number of refugees, especially after the fall of Jajce, and the expelled Croats left, whereas the expelled Muslims stayed on, which caused imbalance and various incidents so that the Muslims that were expelled from other areas and that stayed on in this region, many of them were able-bodied men. The Prosecution claims that the first serious conflict between the Muslims and Croats occurred in October 1992, and he is right as regards the date of that first conflict, but that first conflict did not occur in the territory of Vitez but, rather, in Novi Travnik, and it broke out because of control over a gas station and a hotel; and because of this conflict, the command of the 3rd Corps of the BH army issued an order for setting up barricades on the Vitez-Busovaca road at Ahmici next to -- and also next to the Grbavica building construction enterprise called Bosna. It is quite incredible that this first conflict in Vitez and Ahmici, that the initiators of that conflict -- that the initiation of that conflict should be attributed to the Croatian side, even though there is no question that the barricades were put up by the Muslims. Finally, the roadblock at Ahmici was set up by a Territorial Defence unit from Ahmici. This roadblock, in addition to the people from Ahmici, was manned by members of the Territorial Defence from Vrhovine, who came to assist the people from Ahmici. After the setting up of this barricade or roadblock, a motor vehicle of the military -- HVO Military Police was stopped there and the vehicle was confiscated, and four military policemen who were in the vehicle were disarmed and their weapons were seized from them. Before the outbreak of this conflict, in order to move the roadblock from the road, negotiations were conducted, and when those talks failed the members of the HVO Military Police, with the assistance of a HVO unit from Busovaca, which was moving along the road to Jajce, this road being blocked by the roadblock, they removed this roadblock after a couple of hours of fighting. It is important to note, in connection with this conflict, that the Croatian part of the inhabitants of Ahmici did not participate and, therefore, neither did our clients Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. But we should also remember that their houses were not next to the road or on the other side of the road, and this part of the village was known as Donji Ahmici, but, rather, their houses were in the central part of Ahmici, the part known as Grabovi. In connection with this conflict, the Vitez HVO blocked the Territorial Defence staff. And when I talk about the Territorial Defence, I'm referring to the Muslim segment of the armed forces which were accommodated in the secondary school centre in Vitez, and the BH army attacked and surrounded the staff of the HVO Operative Zone in the village of Kruscica, a village with a majority Muslim population. When this conflict ended on the 22nd of October, 1992, the HVO command for central Bosnia moved to the town of Vitez, was transferred there, and the headquarters of the Territorial Defence moved to Stari Vitez. After this conflict, in January 1993, another conflict occurred, this time in Busovaca, which is some ten kilometres from Vitez. On that occasion, the BH army set up a checkpoint in Kacuni and intersected communication between Vitez and the Lepenica valley and Kiseljak, a communication which was of strategic importance to the HVO. Where this communication was interrupted, the BH army attacked the Croatian villages who would -- which were destroyed and ethnically cleansed. And in a locality called Dusina, the first massacre of civilians in Central Bosnia occurred, the first one in the war between the Muslims and Croats. In the course of our case, we shall show, with the help of photographs and video recording, the extent of the destruction in this area. In the month of April 1993, fresh incidents occurred when the BH army attacked, captured the command staff of the HVO in both Novi Travnik and Vitez. On the 8th of April, 1993, a conflict occurred in Novi Travnik because of Croatian flags there were hoisted prior to Easter, and on the 12th of April, 1993, several HVO soldiers were captured and beaten up. On the 13th of April, 1993, in Novi Travnik and Travnik, four HVO officers were kidnapped. On the 14th of April, 1993, an attempt was made at the life of Darko Kraljevic, the commander of a unit known as Vitezovi. On the 15th of April, in Zenica, the escort of HVO Commander Totic were murdered, and he himself was taken into custody. On that same day, in Zenica, all exits were blocked from the town so that nobody could leave or come to Zenica. On that same day, the 15th of April, 1993, an armed conflict occurred at Kuber, Kuber being a strategic feature at the meeting place of Busovaca, Vitez and Zenica, a position from which, with the help of telescopes, one can see what is happening both in Vitez and in Busovaca and in Zenica, so that on the occasion of this conflict, two HVO members were wounded. Due to all these events, the commander of the Operative Zone, General Tihomir Blaskic, issued three orders which will be tendered into evidence during our case, raising the HVO to the highest level of alert and ordering defence along all frontlines in the event of a Muslim attack. On the 16th of April, 1993, at about 5.30 a.m., conflicts broke out in a number of localities, and allow me to list them. At the approaches to Stari Vitez, and Stari Vitez housed at the time at least 250 BH army, this would be roughly the strength of a battalion, who then and later defended Stari Vitez which, until the end of the war, remained in Muslim hands. Then there was a conflict in Kruscica, a village near Vitez, which also remained under Muslim control, whereas the Croats were expelled from that village and their houses were burned. The village of Donja Veceriska with a mixed population, and the battle over this village went on for several days, and eventually the village was captured by Croats but there were casualties in the fighting on both sides. Then the village of Gacice, again with mixed population, and on the 16th of April, '93 there were no conflicts in that village but there were no -- negotiations which went on for four days. And after these failed, fighting broke out which was won by the Croats. The village of Poculica, which had a majority Croatian population after the 16th of April, 1993, was captured by Muslims, a part of the Croats were expelled, a part captured and Croatian homes were burned down. In the villages of Preocica, Sivrino Selo, and Nadioci and Stari Bila, on the 16th of April, 1993 there were no combat operations, so we don't know why the Prosecutor has included them in the indictment as localities where, on the 16th of April, 1993, there were armed conflicts. Regarding the question as to whether Ahmici, Santici and Pirici were military targets or not, and whether they were defended, or to be more precise, whether any military grouping was -- of the BH army was stationed there, we shall present evidence to show that control of the road passing through Ahmici was of major strategic significance for the HVO, and we believe that we have managed already to prove that strategic importance up to a point when hearing the Prosecution witness Colonel Watters, whose unit was stationed as part of UNPROFOR in the immediate vicinity of Vitez. Though at the beginning he claimed that it was not a strategic goal, in the end he admitted that it was after all. In the course of the presentation of our case, when we present evidence to show that in Santici, Ahmici and Pirici members of the BH army were present and that they were of a strengthened company size, that was there was about 180 men. At the same time, we will attempt to prove that that unit also had a radio transmitter for contact with higher commands, with their own headquarters, that they also had a warehouse of weapons and ammunition, and the company itself belonged to a battalion, the command of which was stationed in Preocica. And the battalion, together with its company, was a component part of the 325th Mountain Brigade of the BH army. In order to show that there was no discriminatory behaviour towards Muslims, to use a simplified term, we will attempt to prove that both the civilian and military authorities of the HVO sought to prevent incidents and any crimes in the area under its control. After presenting evidence regarding the background of the developments in Vitez and the surroundings, since the Prosecution has not specified a single act on the part of the accused which can be described as negative in relation to the Muslims, we will have to show what the attitude of the accused towards the Muslims was, as each individual is a multi-layered personality. We shall first try to illustrate the kind of -- the way in which they behaved at work, that is the dynamite factory where both Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic were employed. We will show that there was no discrimination towards the Muslims. And virtually until the 16th of April -- or, rather, the 15th of April, they continued working in that factory regularly. But the Muslims did not lose their jobs just because they were Muslims or were they laid off, something that the former Yugoslavia invented, that is sending workers home until the factory resumed operations, but we will show that Croats were laid off too, among others Mirjan Kupreskic. But Mirjan Kupreskic was not the only Croat laid off, there were several, and, therefore, the situation in the economy was such that it affected equally members of all ethnic groups even before the conflict that I have referred to broke out. Then we will also illustrate the kind of behaviour the Kupreskic brothers demonstrated in their private lives, and we will see that they had friends among the Muslims, that they exchanged visits, that the Muslims were to come and visit them on Christmas, and they would visit their friends, Muslims, for the Bajram holidays. I hope I pronounce that word properly because I'm not very familiar with it. So that we will show that in their private lives too they were in no way discriminatory towards Muslims just because they were Muslims, but on the contrary, that there were Muslims whom they considered even closer than other people who belonged to their ethnic group, in religious and ethnic terms. We will also show how they spent their free time. Both Kupreskic brothers were members of a folklore society. It was called, in those days, a culture and art society, where folk songs and dances were performed, and Zoran was a kind of leader there. This was a society in which both Croats, Serbs and Muslims participated. The dances and songs were both Muslim, Croat and Serbian, and when they performed they would dress in costumes, including fezzes, and we will show you photographs to illustrate this as well as videotapes of these performances. Finally, we will show what kind of people they were as the neighbours of Muslims, though we don't need much proof because there is sufficient evidence from the witness testimony -- the witness that had the victims in his home. I think he was not a protected witness, so I can mention his name. What happened in Sakib Ahmic's house, and he himself said in court that he never had any problems with them as neighbours, and that he never heard or saw them do anything bad to any Muslims or to say anything nasty to somebody just because he was a Muslim. That is how we have conceived our case with respect to the persecution count. The second part of the indictment, in relation to the Kupreskic brothers, has to do with the events that occurred in the Ahmic family home. It is difficult for us to present evidence about the events in that house, because we weren't there. We only learned subsequently of the tragedy that occurred in that house. However, what we can offer in evidence is what we did -- what was done on the eve of these events, that is the evening of the 15th and the early morning hours of the 16th. I think the other things are not relevant, even though we could offer evidence in that regard as well. The Kupreskic brothers did not know, on 15th of April, that a conflict broke out on the 16th, and in order to confirm that, one of the Kupreskic brothers worked in the factory on the 15th, that is, Zoran did. And Mirjan, who was -- who had been temporarily laid off, he was in his store, and we will prove that he was working that day, that he was in the company of some people, and some beer was drunk at that time, and nobody knew that any conflict would break out the following day because had they known, this would have been addressed, and it was never mentioned that any conflict would break out in the village of Ahmici that following day. We will also offer evidence that in the evening hours of the 15th of April, the Kupreskic brothers were at their cousin's, whose wife, the day before, had arrived from Germany by plane via Split, and she will also supply the aeroplane ticket. Had it been known there would be a conflict the following day, this cousin would definitely not have brought his wife and children back home to be there in the middle of the fighting. We would also prove who and when brought the notice for evacuation of the civilian population, and we can say now that Dragan Vidovic is going to speak to that. Along with a notice of the removal of civilians, he also brought information about the attack of the Bosnian army. As far as the evacuation of civilians is concerned, Your Honours, you have had an opportunity to listen to a number of Prosecution witnesses who spoke about the evacuation of civilians which had also taken place before. As far as our evidence is concerned, that is, the evidence with respect to the Kupreskic brothers, you have to bear in mind that they were in middle Ahmici. It is not -- it is -- they were up in the hill. The civilians who were notified were along the road. We don't know when all these people were notified. Each of the defendants will have to prove when the notice of evacuation reached them. We will also present evidence as to the route that they took, that is Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, when they evacuated their families. They also helped a refugee family be evacuated. At first, this family did not want to go along with them, believing that it was a false alarm. We will also present evidence as to the shelter which was used at the time and how long the Kupreskics stayed in this location without taking part in any armed conflict, and we will present evidence on all these details. Let me address a further point. This Tribunal, as I was able to glean from the Tadic case, uses precedents, which is in the tradition of the common law system. However, this Tribunal does not operate on the basis of common law but, rather, based on the French system, which means that the Prosecution and the Judges are under the same umbrella. Let me point to a problem here. The original indictment which was issued in this same case, which was confirmed by this Trial Chamber, referred almost exclusively to the 16th of April. It didn't refer to any other time period. After the defendants had surrendered, one of the indicted persons, Katava, provided an alibi through one of the Prosecution witnesses, Dr. Mujezinovic, who had already given this alibi to him in the Blaskic case, but since it was provided by a Muslim person was not questioned. After the Katava alibi was confirmed for the 16th of April, the Prosecution dropped the indictment against him. Following that, the indictment was amended based on the same facts because the Prosecution did not come up with any additional facts, at least not with respect to the other accused, and then it widened it, not specifying the date in October '92, so we can assume that it means the 1st of October until the end of April. So where is this principle that all cases should be treated in the same way? And so this is an objection that the Defence has with respect to the Prosecution. You may be left with the impression that I have spent too much time focusing on the events outside of Ahmici, even outside of the Vitez area; however, the majority of locations which we have touched upon are in the surrounding area, so all the evidence which we will be providing is within the ambit of the charges brought by the Prosecution. As far as the state of mind of the indicted, we believe that it is very relevant to show what was going on in and around Ahmici. In Ahmici, practically there were no conflicts until the 16th, and had there not been any conflicts in the surrounding area, without this basis in fact, how were they to believe that this attack would take place so that they would go back to their families. If we prove that there were attacks by Muslims in the areas outside of Ahmici which are close enough, that is, within a radius of about 10 kilometres, then we argue that information which they received about the possibility of attack did play in a particular way in their awareness of the situation that was present in Ahmici at that time. This concludes my remarks, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we should now take a 20-minute break, and then we will move on. I understand that Counsel Radovic spoke both for Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, so the next one will be counsel for Vlatko Kupreskic, I imagine. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Your Honours, my client, Vlatko Kupreskic, was accused in Count 1 and 12 through 15 of the indictment. In Count 1, he is charged that along with the other accused, in a manner described in the indictment, he took part in the persecution of the Bosnian Muslims of Ahmici and that he committed a crime against humanity. In Counts 12 through 15, Vlatko Kupreskic is charged with the murder of a member of the Pezer family, Fata Pezer, and he was charged with the wounding of Dzenana Pezer, which is a crime against humanity and a violation of the laws and customs of war. The Defence will argue that Vlatko Kupreskic did not commit any of the crimes with which he is charged in the indictment, and the Defence will argue the following: With respect to Count 1 of the indictment, the Defence will not present evidence whether there was a persecution of Bosnian Muslims in the village of Ahmici but will only provide evidence that Vlatko Kupreskic played no role in the conflict which took place in the village of Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993, or in the events preceding it, or in the events that had any causal link with those events. As far as the Counts 12 through 15 are concerned, we will offer evidence that Vlatko Kupreskic lived in the village together with his Muslim neighbours, that he was a good neighbour, that he never showed any ill will or that he ever did any harm to anyone. We will also show that Vlatko Kupreskic had a heart problem, that he was never a member of any armed formations, that he was never in uniform or that he ever carried arms. We will also provide evidence that Vlatko Kupreskic was never a member of any political party and that he never formally or informally expressed his political views. We will also show that in the relevant time period, Vlatko Kupreskic was engaged in his professional work, that is, as a salesperson in his own store, both before and during the war. We will also show that Vlatko Kupreskic had no authority, that he never had an opportunity to take part in any preparation for the conflict of 16th April, 1993, because he, in no capacity, could take part in these preparations. With respect to the evidence offered by the Prosecution against Vlatko Kupreskic, pointing that Mr. Kupreskic was seen in front of the Hotel Vitez on the 15th of April and that he was seen with a group of soldiers on the 15th of April, through which the Prosecution is trying to show that he had some knowledge about the events that were to happen on the 16th of April, the Defence is going to provide evidence that on the 14th and 15th of April, 1993, Vlatko Kupreskic was on a business trip abroad and that he only returned to Ahmici on the evening of the 15th of April, 1993. The Defence will show that Vlatko Kupreskic was not in Ahmici on the eve of these events so that he was in no position to have any relevant knowledge about the preparations, and that the witnesses who claim to have seen him at that period of time could objectively not have done so. We will also present evidence through other witnesses who will testify about the accused's stay abroad in the relevant time period, and we will provide a number of documents which will show that the accused Vlatko Kupreskic simply had no reasons to be involved in the persecution of the Bosnian Muslims with which he is charged in the indictment. As far as the legal issues regarding this case are concerned, the Defence will call a Judge from the Supreme Court of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina who will address the issues of civilian persecution, and he will cite a specific judgement of the Supreme Court of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina whereby the Defence will prove that no person can be found guilty without proof of their state of mind. The Defence will develop its defence in two parts. In the first part, we will show that on the 16th of April, 1993, Vlatko Kupreskic was not present in the location as mentioned in Counts 12 through 15, that at the time of the commission of these crimes, he was in a different area, that he was in a shelter for the civilian and the elderly, that is, at that time he was in the shelter which was more than one kilometre away from the location which is mentioned in the indictment. The witnesses which will be called to testify in this regard were in this shelter at that time. During the presentation of evidence of the Prosecution, a witness identified these persons as those whom he saw going to that shelter. As far as Counts 12 through 15 are concerned, the second aspect of the defence will go in a direction to show that the events could not have occurred in the way the indictment has specified and that Fata Peter’s murder and the wounding of Dzenana Pezer did not happen in the way described in the indictment. In that respect, we will call some Muslim witnesses who were moving along in the same group with the ones that were the victims, and a videotape is also going to be offered. Through witnesses and the videotape, we will also show where the body of Fata Pezer was found, which will be compared to Witness F's statement, who, on the map in Exhibit 101, showed the location where Fata Peter’s body lay. The Defence will show that this incident happened in a location which is not visible from the house of Vlatko Kupreskic, so that the victims could not have been hit in the way as specified by the indictment and that the witnesses could not have seen Vlatko Kupreskic's house from their vantage point or could they see the persons who allegedly were in front of the house and shooting. The Defence will also use a ballistics expert as well as a physician, and from their findings, it will be shown that the location at which the body was found and the victim who was wounded and will show that these victims could not have been hit by small arms from Vlatko Kupreskic's house. With respect to the Prosecution witness who is the only one who identified Vlatko Kupreskic and placed him in the location as specified in Counts 12 through 15, the Defence will call an expert witness who will show that such identification under the circumstances was not possible. The Defence will not offer any evidence that members of the army were in Vlatko Kupreskic's house and that shots came from that house, but it will show that the army did forcibly enter that house, that it partially ransacked it as a tactical position, and it will also show that Vlatko Kupreskic was not in the house but only Franjo Kupreskic, his father, who is the owner of this house. The Defence will also show that Vlatko Kupreskic in no way is responsible for the acts with which he was charged, that objectively he could not have committed any of these crimes, and that the Prosecution evidence, which were going to show his involvement in the events of 16 April, 1993 cannot stand. During the presentation of evidence, the witnesses who will speak of the two particular facts of these events will also speak to -- will also be the character witnesses for Vlatko Kupreskic. We will limit ourselves to the relevant evidence without wasting the Trial Chamber's time, and we hope that all our evidence will be presented within one working week. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Krajina. Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, in my introductory remarks, and I will be brief, I will refer to the opening statement of my colleague Ranko Radovic regarding the counts in the indictment. The Defence of Drago Josipovic did file a pre-trial brief which provides an overview of its position and intent of the Defence in his regard. I'm going to first address the general provisions of the indictment, and I want to point out that we will present witnesses which will show that he did not take part in any preparations, that he did not arm himself, and also that he did not take part in the evacuation of Croatian civilians on the eve of the attack. The witnesses will also show that it is not true that Drago Josipovic shot civilians, and witnesses will also testify that Drago Josipovic did not persecute Bosnian Muslims on the ethnic, political or religious basis, that he organised or planned the attack in order to drive the Muslims out of Ahmici. Drago Josipovic was at the bottom of the hierarchy. He was just a member of the village guard. There were commanders in the village, and these commanders were directly linked to the Defence Department, which is part of the Crisis Staff that is part of the HVO government. Since the charges were dropped against Ivica Santic, who was the chief of the Crisis Staff and who, through the office -- defence office had contacts with the village commanders, we will show that Drago Josipovic in no way could participate in the planning and organising of the attack against Muslims in the village of Ahmici and in the surrounding villages, because the surrounding villages were also -- like Santici, were also under the control of the Crisis Staff, if there was enough control. Also, we will show that the Muslims provoked the first conflict which took part on the 20th October, 1992 by interrupting the communication between Travnik and Busovaca. The Defence will show that the HVO did not systematically attack with majority Muslim population in the Lasva River Valley, and that a number of civilians were wounded and killed.
