The Defence will show that there was an armed conflict on 16th April, 1993 between the HVO and the BH army, and the witnesses will testify that BH army defence in Ahmici was organised, that they were armed and that they had a defence plan. The Defence will also show that the killed Muslims were not all civilian, but that among the killed there were also members of the BH army. The Defence will show that Drago Josipovic was not trained to take part in any military operations, and it will show that he did not take part in attacks against civilians and certain structures as was -- as charged in the indictment. The Defence will also show that Drago Josipovic was a member of no party, and he was employed, and it will show that he was at his workplace the day before the attack, that is on the 15th of April, 1993. The Defence will also call witnesses who will show that Drago Josipovic could not have committed crimes in three different locations, that is in two locations, and that he could not have been himself in three separate places. The sequence of events which are indicated in the indictment, and the distances between these locations, show that Drago Josipovic could not have committed a crime at Ramo Ahmic's house where four persons were killed, and at the same time be at Musafer Puscul's house, who was killed, and we will prove that he was at Anto Papic's house, which is the third location. A witness which had been offered by the Prosecution will confirm that Drago Josipovic was there and this is at a time right after her son had been killed. The Defence of Drago Josipovic will also show that he did not lock up a Muslim prisoner in the Ogrijev company. We will also provide photographic evidence which will show that the Bosnian Muslim could have left this guardhouse, because it had a window which was open from within, and he could have left this house and could have climbed the fence. And the witnesses will also show that the fence had a door, a gate, which was open. As far as the specific count of the -- counts of the indictment, the Defence will show that at the time when Musafer Puscul was killed and his house was set on fire, that Drago Josipovic was at Anto Papic's house, and witnesses will confirm -- which will confirm the testimony of a witness which had already been produced by the Prosecution. The Defence will also show that the statement of the witness who charged him, that this witness is not credible enough. The Defence witnesses will further show that Drago Josipovic has positive character traits, that he socialised with Muslims at work and he had Muslim neighbours. He had no criminal record. He assisted Muslims, even providing them financial aid. The Defence will also show that Drago Josipovic did go to the international organisations and to the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that he volunteered to come here to prove that he did not commit any war crimes, and we believe that this will all serve the justice, and, Your Honours, this is all I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Susak. Counsel Puliselic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours. The amended indictment dated 9 February, 1998, the Prosecutor charges, under Count 1 of this indictment, Dragan Papic for participation in the persecution of Bosnian Muslims on political, religious or racial grounds, which is qualified as a crime against humanity under Article 5(h) of the statute of the International Criminal Tribunal. In my opening statement, I shall try, as succinctly as possible, to present to this Trial Chamber what the Defence of Dragan Papic intends to show by the presentation of evidence and the calling of witnesses, and that is that the accused Dragan Papic did not commit the crime he is charged with in the indictment. In my opening statement, I wish to join in the statements made by other Defence counsel regarding the general facts and which I will not refer to so as to avoid repetition. By the examination of witnesses and the presentation of other evidence, the Defence will focus on the events linked to the first armed conflict which occurred on the 20th of October, 1992, and in particular, on the events linked to the second armed conflict which occurred on the 16th of April, 1993, but also on some other events in the period in between those two dates. The Defence, in its opening statement, wishes again to refer to its points of fact and law presented in its written briefs of the 10th of November, 1998, and we will not elaborate those points in this opening statement. The Defence will attempt to prove that Dragan Papic is not a nationalist fanatic, that he did not participate in any way in the systematic killing of Bosnian Muslims, the destruction of their homes and the expulsion of civilian Muslims, that he did not prepare or assist in the crimes committed against Muslims, his neighbours, and that he did not evacuate his family on the eve of the conflict because he was not aware of the events that would occur on the 16th of April. We shall also present evidence to show that Dragan Papic did not in any way participate in the planning, organisation or ordering of the persecution of Bosnian Muslims on political, racial or religious grounds. We will present evidence to show that in the period from October 1992 until April 1993, Dragan Papic did not commit any criminal acts in order to persecute his neighbours from Ahmici. By the examination of witnesses, we shall show Dragan Papic in his real light, not as a cold-blooded, malicious criminal as he is portrayed in the indictment, but as an ordinary human being with his virtues and shortcomings. We will show that he is a sociable person, a person who likes other people and who is ready to assist everyone. There is no doubt that a person of this kind could not have coffee and joke with his neighbours Muslims, today repair their cars and bring milk for their children on a daily basis, and the next day be transformed into another person, abandon them in cold blood, and even be an active participant in their persecution and killing. We will show that Dragan Papic is not a monster but a man with a soul, who liked to joke, and to socialise and to be friends, with other people, regardless of their ethnic affiliation. At the beginning of the war and the armed conflict with the Serbs, Dragan Papic, in addition to his clothing as a forester, would often wear black and camouflage clothing, and he would often combine these uniforms with civilian clothing. And the Defence wishes to underline that in the area affected by war, many young people wore uniforms, but this did not necessarily mean that they were members of organised military units. This was a widespread phenomena among the youth, regardless of their ethnic and religious feelings. This was the fashion. It was something that was in. Dragan Papic wore no insignia, and he would wear a camouflage or a black uniform even when he went to work as a forester. Occasionally he would carry a rifle because he moved in the woods where there were wild animals, and he needed to protect himself. The Defence wishes to underline that Dragan Papic never used that rifle to threaten anyone, never mind to kill or injure anyone. No one who speaks the truth can say that Papic was a person prone to quarrels and conflicts. Dragan Papic never participated in any physical fights. In the house of his father Ivo, where he lived too, many neighbours would come. His father was a skilled craftsman. He was employed in the water supply system in Vitez, on maintenance, and in his free time he would set up plumbing for his neighbours and friends when they asked him to do it. Ivo Papic installed the plumbing in the mosque in Ahmici. Dragan, in his free time, if he was not repairing cars he would be assisting his father. We will also show that both Croats and Muslims would come to their home, and not any one of the members of the household distinguished people according to their national ethnicity or religion. Dragan Papic was in charge of civil defence and occasionally meetings would be held in his home. On the other hand, Dragan Papic's hobby was mechanics and he was particularly well versed in automobile engines, and that is why in front of his house there were cars of his friends, and neighbours and acquaintances, because he would repair those cars in his free time. When he got married in 1991, he continued to live in his father's home, as he had no other choice. The closeness of the hostilities and the danger of Serb attacks formed adult males to organise night watches so as to prepare in time for movements of Serbian military units, and all this in the -- in order to defend their families and homes. At first these guards were composed of both Croats and Muslims, until the first conflict when the Muslims separated. Without having any idea of what would happen early in the morning of the 20th of October, Dragan Papic and the other members of his household were awakened by powerful shooting. The father was not at home, he was in Split at the time, so Dragan took over care of the family. So he took his mother, sister and wife to nearby Donja Rovna, south of his house. We will show that on the road to Donja Rovna he encountered Nenad Santic, who, among other things, was in charge of the evacuation of the local people. Nenad Santic said to Papic that he should take over the small mortar, 16-millimetre mortar, the manning of which Dragan Papic learnt about while doing his military service in the JNA, and to take it to a hill called Neretva near Donja Rovna in order to control the possible arrival of BH army units from the direction of Gornja Rovna, Pezici and Kajmakovici. Actually, the conflict that occurred in the early morning, and due to which Dragan Papic was on his way to Donja Rovna where he met Nenad Santic, broke out between forces of the BH army and the HVO over the roadblock on the main road close to the Catholic cemetery, a roadblock set up by the Muslims to prevent passage of HVO units which were on their way to assist HVO units in Jajce who were fighting Serb forces. We will see that on that day, the 20th of October, 1992, Dragan Papic was throughout at Neretva and he did not use the mortar because that was not necessary, as BH army units were -- did not come from the area which he was assigned to control. Witnesses will testify about all this, and especially the witness whose house is just below the position where Dragan Papic was. This witness saw Dragan Papic throughout that day, that is from the early morning until late in the afternoon he saw him in the area of Neretva. Therefore, Dragan Papic could not have simultaneously shot from the window of his house with an automatic rifle against his neighbour's house, and then from a wood with an anti-aircraft gun. On that day no one could have used a sniper from Papic's house because no one was in the house at the time from the members -- none of the members of the family. After this conflict over the roadblock in which the Croat inhabitants of Ahmici did not participate at all and the conflict in which several -- in addition to several Muslim houses, several Croatian houses were hit and damaged, and a witness will talk about this, the village guards continued to be held but no longer jointly. Dragan Papic continued to work in Sumarija, and he would occasionally keep watch at night until the 16th of April, 1993, when, in the morning, all the inhabitants of Ahmici were woken up by the sound of shooting. Dragan's wife was about to give birth, so that he took her, his mother and sister immediately through the woods to Donja Rovna, whereas his father and brother found temporary shelter in the woods. After finding accommodation for the women of the family, he remained upon orders on guard on the left bank of the River Lasva with two other men. He spent the whole day there on guard duty as well as during the next ten days or so until his wife gave birth. The guards rested in the house of the late Pero Ljubas, and throughout that period, they were not allowed to move away from that area. The old Radakov Most bridge became a very important facility because it provided the only connection between Busovaca and Vitez in those days, a road that went across the meadows, along the right bank of the Lasva Valley, since the main road could not be used because of the machine gun nests of BiH army units at Buhine Kuca about two kilometres east of Vitez. Witnesses will testify to this, witnesses who took part in guard duty together with Dragan Papic at Radak's bridge. Since Dragan Papic, on the 16th of April, 1993, and the days that followed, was constantly on guard duty at such an important strategic feature, it is quite obvious that he could not simultaneously have been in the Muslim houses he is alleged to have been in. We will also show that an anti-aircraft gun, machine gun, or any other such weapon never was in his house nor near his house nor was that house ever used as a fortress for shooting from, as the Prosecution would have us believe, but that it was an ordinary family home inhabited by three women, Dragan's brother, who was a minor, and his father, an elderly man. In addition, Dragan's wife was in advanced pregnancy at the time. Therefore, the Defence will show that in the period covered by the indictment, Dragan Papic never committed any such serious crime as a crime against humanity as alleged under Article 5 of the Statute nor did he commit any such crime before or after that period. Finally, the Defence would like to say that considerable effort has been invested to bring to court Muslim witnesses who are friends and acquaintances of the Papic family and who are very familiar with the kind of person Dragan Papic is and who know well that Dragan did not participate in this crime in any way, but due to their own security and the safety of their own families, in spite of promised protective measures, they could not decide to come and testify in court; namely, those persons live in fear that they could lose their jobs, their apartments, if it was to be learnt that they had testified as Defence witnesses. That is why Dragan Papic's counsel does not wish to expose Dragan's friends, Muslims, to any fears, and particularly not to any possible consequences. In spite of this handicap for Dragan Papic's Defence counsel, we do believe that with the help of witnesses and the other evidence we have, we will manage to prove his innocence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Puliselic. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence counsel of Vladimir Santic, in his written brief of the 4th of November, 1998, has already presented its intentions regarding the presentation of evidence in its case. In this opening statement, we wish merely to highlight some of the key points of those positions of ours. In the first place, I wish to remind Your Honours that according to the indictment of the Prosecutor of the International Tribunal dated 9th of March, 1998, and which was subsequently amended, the accused Vladimir Santic has been charged that, together with the other accused, as specified in Count 1 and in paragraphs 9, 10, 20, and 21, that this accused committed a crime against humanity by committing persecution on political, racial, or religious grounds, which is punishable under Article 5(H) of the Statute of the International Tribunal. If we examine closely all the Prosecutor's allegations contained in these counts and if we assess them in the context of the evidence presented, then the same objections may be made which Attorney Radovic has already made and which the Defence of Vlado Santic will not repeat so as not to tire the Trial Chamber, but will, through the evidence presented regarding the general allegations, show that Vladimir Santic could not have, in any way, carried out any one of the acts attributed to him by the Prosecutor. Not one of the Prosecution witnesses claimed that Vladimir Santic assisted in the preparation of the attack, that he attacked civilians and their property, that he persecuted Bosnian Muslims on political, racial, or religious grounds. Not one of the witnesses has claimed that he supports the intention, deliberately and systematically, to kill Bosnian Muslims. That is why, by presenting evidence, the Defence will demonstrate the real attitude of the accused Vladimir Santic to the events covered by the Prosecutor in his amended indictment. The Prosecutor, in his pre-trial brief, had only one sentence in which they said that Vladimir Santic participated in an incident of killing, and nothing more than that. The Defence, by presenting its evidence, will show that this thesis of the Prosecution is untenable; namely, as indicated in items 16 to 19 of the indictment, that Vladimir Santic had any connection with this murder. For if we examine closely all the relevant evidence of the Prosecution and particularly the testimony of Witness EE, on the basis of which the Prosecution bases its charges exclusively, the Defence will, by calling a number of witnesses, draw the Court's attention to the fact that the testimony of this witness is not credible proof and that it does not provide a basis for the conclusion that Vladimir Santic committed this crime. The Defence recalls that in the course of the presentation of evidence by the Prosecution, it had drawn attention to the reasons which call in question the credibility of this Prosecution witness, which is the only witness for this act, and that already at the time we had submitted a brief in support of our allegation that the statement of this witness is not acceptable. By calling its witnesses, the Defence will simply confirm what it has already documented through its briefs and by hearing this witness, who was also accused by that witness together with Santic, and this witness claimed that the accused, together with this witness and some other witnesses, committed the murder of a person close to her and then devastated his property. Therefore, by hearing the testimony of these witnesses who will be speaking about their relationship with the Prosecution witness, the Defence wants to show that under no circumstances, in view of all this, can the testimony of that witness be accepted, of course, taking into consideration the numerous other factors that the Defence has drawn attention to, saying that this witness testimony, which is the only testimony the Prosecution has in corroboration of these charges, cannot be trusted. Finally, in the course of its case, the Defence will show that the accused Vladimir Santic was not linked to the events in the indictment nor could he have been linked to them because at the time when the Prosecution alleges he was in Ahmici, he, in fact, was elsewhere, and therefore, physically, nor in any other way, could he have influenced the course of events nor the crimes committed. Through the testimony of witnesses, the Defence of Vladimir Santic will prove that Vladimir Santic was, at the relevant time, in the Vitez Hotel where a unit was stationed, a unit that he belonged to, and that throughout that day, he was in the hotel, which will be corroborated by documents, some of which have already been admitted, and some will be tendered in our case, that is, the orders of the commands of this area, that is, the orders of General Blaskic, from which it is visible that no offensive operations had been planned and that, accordingly, Vladimir Santic, together with the unit that was securing the command post, was in the hotel on that day. Therefore, the Defence submits that this point is of the greatest relevance regarding the alleged responsibility of Vladimir Santic. Finally, the Defence reserves the right, in accordance with Rule 73 ter, to revise the proposed list of witnesses, as it has done in its documents submitted to the Prosecution and the Court. That is all, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we are in a position to call our first witness, but before we do so, let me go back to an issue raised by Counsel Puliselic, who rightly pointed out that in some way he is at a disadvantage because of the impossibility for him to call some witnesses who might testify on behalf of his client but fear to come forward to testify because of possible pressure or retaliation by other members of the same ethnic community. I wonder whether Counsel Puliselic has explored all the possibilities that are offered. For instance, I think we are prepared to call those witnesses as Court witnesses. I wonder whether you have discussed this possibility with them. Two possibilities: Court witnesses or we could, as sort of extrema ratio, use video conference, which is, of course, less helpful, I think, and less in line with our own practice. Did you discuss this matter with these potential witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: I did, but they are simply afraid, and as I mentioned in my opening statement, that because of their fear, we do not wish to exert any further pressure on them. We realised that they were fearful regardless of everything we told them of the various possibilities, the protective measures; however, there is a fear among them, and we do not wish to influence them any further to change their decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I am afraid then we don't have any means of calling those witnesses. Yes, Counsel Radovic? Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The problem that colleague Puliselic has mentioned exists in our case too, the Kupreskic brothers, because of their membership in the culture and arts society in which they sang and danced, they had many friends among the Muslims. When we were in Vitez, some of them responded to our call for a conversation, and we spoke to them. Initially, they said they needed time to think it over, whether to agree to come and testify or to testify in any other way because we told them of all the possibilities we have at our disposal to hear their testimony. However, after thinking things over, all of them refuse to testify, giving the explanation that their families, some of whom had also been killed in Ahmici, and that no one of their families would forgive them if they had come to testify about the events in Ahmici in favour of the Croats, even though they personally were convinced, at least as far as the Kupreskic brothers are concerned, because they were the ones I discussed with these witnesses, were not guilty. This went so far that I spoke to one Muslim in Travnik, and he doesn't even know anything about what happened in Ahmici, but after those events, he spoke to Mirjan Kupreskic, and the conversation consisted of the following, that Mirjan told him that he didn't know what the Court was charging him with, so this would be evidence to show that he was surprised. He probably would not have been surprised if he had known -- if he had done something. And even this witness asked for time to think it over, and eventually he refused. The only thing we might do is to propose a couple of names of Muslims who might decide to come if they are called as Court witnesses, and maybe we could try that and see whether they would respond to your summons. We would also propose the investigating magistrate of the High Court in Zenica be called as a court witness, the one who examined the protected witness who claimed that she had never made a statement in the Zenica court. That would be my suggestion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So you will then provide the list of names. Yes, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, in this context, I don't know whether you have noticed, but we have submitted to the Court testimonies of character witnesses, several Muslim witnesses, who were willing to come to The Hague to sign their testimonies and subsequently had second thoughts. So maybe on the basis of those statements we could call them into The Hague because they signed those statements and had second thoughts afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: As for character witnesses, we might simply accept the statements, if there is no objection from the Prosecution, so that we don't need to call them to The Hague. If they are only character witnesses, I don't see why we should not. I mean -- as I say, unless the Prosecution has any major objection. But we can leave this matter for later on. Yes, Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Simply regarding this point, Mr. President, I would say a priori there is no objection on the part of the Prosecution against the acceptance of statements, but the position of the Prosecution has to be taken on a case-by-case basis depending on the contents of those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I think this is the right position, of course. On a case-by-case basis, you may object or accept, but I think we would call upon the Defence counsel to indicate the various statements they would like to provide -- we are thinking of character witnesses -- so that the Prosecution is given enough time to consider this matter and see whether they have any objection. If they don't have any objection, they could be admitted into evidence. I think, since we still have half an hour, even a bit more than half an hour, we could probably start with the first witness, that's Zvonimir Cilic. While we are waiting for the witness, I would like to take this opportunity to urge Defence counsel to provide not only a list of witnesses they intend to call the following week but also a list of reserve witnesses as the Prosecution rightly did, so that in case one drops out or we have more time or the testimony is very short, we still have other witnesses to hear. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Before I ask the witness to make the solemn declaration, may I ask you, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, to tell me whether there are any protective measures required for the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No. Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Cilic. Could you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Cilic.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please state for the record when were you born, where you were born, where you work, and so on?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: Can I do all that while sitting?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: I am Zvonimir Cilic, born in 1946, I'm a social worker in Vitez, and I work as a journalist in Slobodna Dalmacija in Split, I live and work in Vitez, I am married with two children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what you did in late 1991? How were you employed?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: I was employed as a social worker in the company Vitezit in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you stop working?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: Officially I did not stop working, but because of the economic crisis which ensued after the break-up of the former Yugoslavia, in my company a certain number of employees had to be temporarily laid off. In other words, they had to stay at home and not come to work. I first was put in a situation like that in late 1991, I was on hold for two months, and then in 1992 this happened again, after which I never went back because I stopped being interested in working there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you do then in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: With a group of friends we started publishing a paper called Lasvanski Glasnik, the Lasva Messenger, which was a monthly magazine. However, the Crisis Staff, which was comprised of both Muslims and Croats, invited me to set up a press service for the press and staff of the Vitez municipality and I agreed. We consisted of five people. There were three Croats and two Muslims. There was myself, two other Croats and two Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: Midhat Varupa, who is a lawyer; and Mohamed Halilovic, who was a teacher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this press service was part of the Crisis Staff or was it a separate service?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: This was a service of a Crisis Staff and also of the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was this Crisis Staff in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: You see, as early as 1991 there were a number problems in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and there was the attack of the former JNA against certain parts of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we were looking for ways to protect citizens in our municipality because the JNA had already occupied some parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina and even some very important communication lines, so the Crisis Staff was set up to deal with those issues. They needed to organise the supply of citizenry, because the food stocks were low and the people were unemployed. They didn't have enough money to pay with, so this wasn't enough supply, so part of the Crisis Staff's function was to try to supply the citizenry and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did both the Croats and the Bosniaks make part of this Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was proportionate. In other words, it reflected the composition of the population of Vitez municipality, and it reflected the results of the elections, and the results of the elections also sort of reflected the composition of the population in the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what was the proportion in terms of different -- of ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: You mean in the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: I may be slightly off, but the Vitez municipality has about 26.000 inhabitants. There were slightly less than 13.000 Croats, slightly over 11.000 Bosniak Muslims, about 1.500 Serbs, about 1.000 Yugoslavs and a couple hundred of others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the composition of the Crisis Staff reflected the ethnic structure. Does that mean that the ethnic structure dictated or the elections dictated this composition?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: It doesn't matter which criteria you take because they overlapped. It was very easy to find the proper key and find the solution which was acceptable for both the Croat and Muslim side, because at the time the relationships were still very good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please just slow down? You speak too fast and so it's hard to interpret.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will try.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first government which was established in the Vitez municipality, as you said, reflected that the Croats and Muslims had pretty much the same numbers.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: If you will allow me -- let me go back to my notes. On the 11th of November, the elections were held and the HDZ got 40.2 per cent, the SDA got 30.7, SDS about 18.6, and then the Youth Movement 2.1 and the Reform Party with the former Prime Minister got 3.9, and there were a couple of other parties which got very little or very few votes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the local government structures, did they also take into account this -- the ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In assigning different posts of the local government, did it also reflect the ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was taken into account. The majority party had to get the top position, so the Croatian candidate got the top spot in the municipality, and the second, which was the President of the executive board. So Ivan Santic was the President from the municipality and the President of the Executive Board was Fuad Kaknjo. He was a member of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the other key positions in the municipal government? Were they also filled by this same criteria?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: All positions which were elected positions were filled in such a way that it reflected the 18 November elections. In other words, that they were equally divided between the two parties which won the elections, that is the HDZ and the SDA, and there were no problems. I just receive a warning to slow down and I'll try to do so. So the representatives of the SDA and the HDZ were represented in the manner that reflected the elections. In other words, the representatives of the Croats and Muslims. And in the beginning, as far as I know, there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as the commander of the Territorial Defence is concerned, who was appointed commander?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: It was the Bosnian Muslims, and I believe Hakija Cengic is his name. He was appointed to that position because he had the proper training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the Territorial Defence? It was this institution that was sort of inherited from the previous systems?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was taken over from the former system. At first, some of these institutions were just kept in place, there was no need to change them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what was the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence, in the former system, was a formation that existed along with the JNA. It was staffed with reserves. It was sort of a reserve corps in case Yugoslavia was attacked, but it also was charged with assisting the population if there was any natural disaster or any such crisis. So it was a reserve aspect of the JNA, the regular army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the Territorial Defence start to be transformed into something that was not just a reserve formation structure but a military structure?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: It started being transformed into a military structure at a time when the first serious problems between Croats and Muslims started appearing in the area where I lived, that is in Lasva River Valley, Vitez, that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what -- where was -- what was the war with the Serbs at that time, first in Croatia and then in this area?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: That's what I had in mind when I said that the Territorial Defence was becoming less and less Croatian and more and more Bosniak Muslim, because it was apparent at that time that Muslims and Croats in Central Bosnia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina overall perceived the JNA aggression or Serbia aggression against Croatia a different way, especially at a time when the JNA, that is the Serbian army, entered the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, when it conducted combat operations from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina against Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the official response of President Izetbegovic, that is, of the official Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the reaction of Alija Izetbegovic may have been a sort of irritant for the Croats, and maybe that's what instilled the first fear in them, because Mr. Izetbegovic several times repeated, "The war in Croatia is not our war." When he said, "Our war," he meant Bosnia and Herzegovina, but for Croats in Bosnia, you couldn't speak of war in Croatia in that way, because we Croats in Bosnia felt that it was our war as well because we saw it as a threat to Bosnia and Herzegovina as well. We saw that it could not be stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the -- when did the Croatian side start organising itself?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: As early as 1991, when the -- when the village of Rama was attacked in Herzegovina. This is a Croatian village, and the Serbian army, which was still called the JNA, ran it over. Then the Croats in Bosnia saw that they needed to get organised, to get prepared, because the sword of war was hanging over it. And we were very anxious about this war, much more so than the Bosnian Muslims were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when was it that any organisation started, and when the Croats started organising themselves and started establishing some military structures?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: In the territory of Vitez municipality, as well as in other areas where the Croats were in majority, started organising village watches in 1991. I don't know if I need to go into what village watches are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: At first these were just groups of citizens, regardless of their ethnic background. If they were mixed villages, let's say Croats and Muslim, they would form joint watches. It consisted of just preventing -- its goal was to prevent anything happening during the night, including simple looting or thefts, because the rule of law had weakened to that extent that it was needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, but could you just slow down a little bit again?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: There were also a number of barracks occupied by the JNA, such as in Novi Travnik, Travnik, Busovaca, Kiseljak. And that was one of the fears for them, the Croatian population, and we also felt in the beginning that the communication lines could be interrupted, blocked suddenly, that certain companies would be taken over. There were a lot of military complexes in Bugojno and Vitez and other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what is the significance of the Vitez company for the military?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: At one point there were three companies. Vitezit was one of the largest facilities for production of explosives and gunpowder in the Balkans. It employed 3.000 people, and it was part of the military industrial complex of the former JNA. It was a significant part of this military industrial complex, because without this company there would be no explosives, or gunpowder or rocket propellants. So it could be said that this was one of the key facilities in the military industrial complex of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the JNA, that is the Bosnian Serbs, attack Vitezit, and when was it attacked?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: Several times Croats, but it was only Croats, who tried to prevent the military equipment and weapons being hauled from Vitezit and from the facilities in Novi Travnik, because the JNA had more and more need for the products of Vitezit and Novi Travnik. In Novi Travnik guns were manufactured and some other military equipment, and as I said, in Vitez it was explosives, and gunpowder and rocket propellants. And we did protect it any way we could. We knew that this was going to go to Croatia and be used against Croats, and the JNA troops were leaving at that time, they were leaving Slovenia and they were getting re-deployed in the area of Central Bosnia. And the factory kept working. What we did was try to prevent all the supplies and this equipment being hauled away, but it was very difficult because JNA were still very strong, very powerful. And a number of officials, military personnel, were still siding with the JNA because they were afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Vitez shelled?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: Yes. The first time when -- first attacked on 26 April, 1992, and the shelling was preceded by the surrender of the Busovaca barracks of the JNA, which was called Draga. The Croatian population and its political structure exerted pressure and Draga was abandoned, and took their -- they had to leave, and they had to leave the equipment behind and there was a lot of it. However, several hours later the JNA planes bombed the area of Busovaca and Vitez. There was some damages in Vitez, and in Busovaca three people were killed, two Croats and one Muslim person, and material damage was also significant. There were several burned buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding the formation of the army, you said that the -- originally, the army started in the form of village guards. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, institutions of the Croatian people were set up in the territory of Vitez municipality in the same way in which they were formed in other places in Bosnia-Herzegovina where the Croats had a majority. Are you referring to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and then the HVO? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the municipal staff begin to be formed?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: The joint municipal staff existed already at the beginning of 1992. At first there were no problems and all the staffs were manned jointly, Crisis Staffs and Defence Staffs. However, at the beginning of 1992, these institutions of the Croatian people were set up, and on the 18th of November, '91 the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, and then in the spring of 1992 the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was happening on the Bosniak side in terms of the formation of the army in this period?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: The Croats were setting up their own units in order to resist the Serb aggression, because already in January '92 the Serbs were close to the Lasva Valley. They had gained control of the Vlasic Mountain, which was dominant in Northern and Central Bosnia, and they had also captured an important strategic feature called Komor on the road between Travnik and Gornji Vakuf, or, rather, on the communication line linking Central Bosnia with Dalmatia, Western Bosnia and Croatia. And this was a signal that we had to organise and resist the Serb aggression, otherwise we would end up in the same way as many other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and many parts of Croatia had ended up by then. Even before the formation of the HVO, these village guards were gradually enlarged and these Crisis Staffs started to be formed. And in Vitez already in October '91 the coordination, organisation and preparation started, though they were still not formal military units, but fear and threats forced people to self organise to form the appropriate bodies and to identify the people who would be capable of preparing and organising defence against the Serbs. And as I said, the threats were obvious because all communications had been intercepted, the supply of food and medicines had become difficult, because of this road linking us to Dalmatia and Croatia was cut off. So we were forced to find other routes at a time of great shortages. We built a road, which was some 30 kilometres long, and instead of using the normal road to Split, which would take us 3 hours, these new roads -- along these new roads it took us 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the HVO get armed?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: The arming started before the HVO. The village guard started mostly with hunting rifles or old weapons -- who knows where people got them from -- but then there was black marketeering too and one could purchase weapons on the black market. An illustration that I could give is people would sell a cow which fed the whole family to buy a gun because they thought this was essential for their survival. More serious arming by the HVO started with the capture of barracks of the former JNA, or maybe it would be better to say that already, in '91, by decision of the official authorities in Sarajevo, all the weapons of the Territorial Defence in Vitez, for instance, these were stored in the Vitezit factory, orders came that the Yugoslav People's Army should take over those weapons; in other words, already in May 1991, the Bosniak and Croat peoples in Central Bosnia were totally disarmed. Earlier, we had certain quantities of high-quality weapons, as the Territorial Defence, but this decision taken in May '91 took all this away from us so that we were left with nothing. About a year later -- or let me be more precise -- on the 3rd of May, 1992, military units -- I can call them that -- of the HVO of Novi Travnik and Vitez, Vitez in particular, assisted by units from Novi Travnik, captured a large arms depot called Slimena, in the territory of Travnik municipality or, rather, at the intersection of three municipalities, Travnik, Novi Travnik, and Vitez. This was the first more serious conflict between the so-called JNA and Croatian units in Central Bosnia when the first Croatian military victims fell, two young men were killed, Ilija Petrovic and Josip Kurevija, and some 15 young men were wounded, but large quantities of weapons were seized, and this later proved to be very important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, these weapons were in the possession of the HVO or the TO as well?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: It was not appropriated only by the HVO even though the HVO and the HOS participated in this operation, but the very next day, a principled agreement was reached that all these weapons seized in Slimena should be shared 50-50 between the Territorial Defence and the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: If I may tender an exhibit on this issue, then we can resume the testimony tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked D17/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could the usher -- oh, yes. The witness has a copy. Fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we have the original of the document now. Do you know who was the commander of the crisis staff of Vitez municipality at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: It was Ivan Santic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise his signature?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: Yes. He has a specific signature, and I would come across it frequently because I was often in attendance at meetings of the crisis staff and later of the HVO government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the stamp you see there, that is the stamp of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the stamp that was still valid at the time for both sides, conditionally speaking, because we didn't really have two sides yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that at that time an order was issued that all the resources taken from TO warehouses, the Travnik maintenance shop, and other facilities be divided up equally between the Territorial Defence of Vitez and the HVO headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: That is what I just said a moment ago in my testimony. This just corroborates my statement. I think there is nothing disputed about this. For a long time after this, the same attitude was applied regarding resources of the Vitezit factory and other resources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we see here, "I order that all resources taken from the TO warehouse," this actually refers to the former TO, from the former system; it is not the TO, the Territorial Defence, that developed later in '92?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR CILIC
utterances.text: If I may say so, I think this is rather a clumsy wording. The TO warehouse really means the JNA warehouse where all the weapons from the municipalities of Central Bosnia had been seized and stored earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I suggest that we can break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will adjourn until tomorrow at 9.00, and tomorrow, as you remember, we will sit only in the morning, from 9.00 to 1.30. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 1.34 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 12th day of January, 1999, at 9.00 a.m. 25
